title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: Napoleon enters Moscow after the brilliant victory at the Moskva; the victory is beyond doubt, since the battlefield remains in French hands. The Russians retreat and abandon their ancient capital. Moscow, overflowing with provisions, weapons, ammunition, and incalculable wealth, is in Napoleon's hands. The Russian army, only half the strength of the French, doesn't make a single attempt to attack for an entire month. Napoleon's position is magnificent. He can either fall on the Russian army with double their strength and destroy it; negotiate a favorable peace; or, if refused, make a threatening move on Petersburg; or even, in case of a setback, fall back to Smolensk or Vilna; or simply stay in Moscow. In short, no special genius would seem necessary to hold the brilliant position the French occupied at that time. All that was needed were very simple, obvious steps: don't let the troops loot, prepare winter clothing (there was enough in Moscow for the whole army), and systematically collect the provisions which, according to French historians, were sufficient to supply the army for six months. Yet Napoleon—that greatest of all geniuses, who historians claim controlled the army—took none of these steps.

Not only did he fail to do any of this, but he used his power to choose the most foolish and ruinous of all available options. Of everything Napoleon might have done—wintering in Moscow, marching on Petersburg or Nizhni-Novgorod, or retreating by a northern or southern route (say, the road Kutuzov later took)—nothing more stupid or disastrous can be imagined than what he actually did. He lingered in Moscow until October, letting the troops plunder the city. Then, hesitating whether to leave a garrison behind, he abandoned Moscow, approached Kutuzov without giving battle, veered right and reached Malo-Yaroslavets, again without trying to break through and take Kutuzov's road, and instead retreated to Mozhaysk along the devastated Smolensk road. Nothing more idiotic could have been devised—or more devastating for the army, as events soon proved. If Napoleon's goal had been to destroy his own army, the most brilliant strategist could hardly have come up with a series of actions that would accomplish it more completely, regardless of anything the Russian army might do.

Napoleon, the man of genius, did this. But to say he destroyed his army because he wanted to, or because he was very stupid, would be as unjust as saying he had brought his troops to Moscow because he wanted to and because he was very clever.
In both cases, his personal actions—having no more force than any individual soldier's—merely coincided with the laws that governed the events.

Historians quite falsely portray Napoleon's abilities as having weakened in Moscow, and they do this only because the results didn't justify his actions. He applied all his skill and strength to do the best he could for himself and his army, just as he had done before and would do again in 1813. His activity during this period was no less remarkable than in Egypt, Italy, Austria, or Prussia. We can't be certain how genuine his genius was in Egypt—where forty centuries looked down on his glory—since the accounts come entirely from the French. We can't accurately assess his genius in Austria or Prussia either, since our information comes from French or German sources, and the mysterious surrender of entire corps and fortresses without a fight naturally inclines Germans to credit his genius as the only explanation. But we, thank God, don't need to invoke his genius to cover up our shame. We have earned the right to look at this matter plainly and simply, and we won't give up that right.

His activity in Moscow was as remarkable and as full of genius as anywhere else. Order after order and plan after plan poured from him, from the moment he entered Moscow until the moment he left. The absence of citizens and a deputation, and even the burning of Moscow, didn't faze him. He never lost sight of his army's welfare, the enemy's movements, the welfare of the Russian people, the direction of affairs in Paris, or the diplomatic considerations surrounding the anticipated peace.
